hints: Look at the shape and electron pairs around the central atom before and after each conversion.
Recall that $\text{NH}_4^+$ is tetrahedral with angle $109.5^\circ$ while $\text{NH}_3$ is pyramidal with angle $107^\circ$.
Compare this to ethene changing from trigonal planar near $120^\circ$ to ethane changing to tetrahedral near $109.5^\circ$, and see what trend is shared.
walkthrough:
**Find the shapes in the first conversion**

Think of $\text{NH}_4^+$ as having 4 bonding pairs and no lone pairs. That gives a perfect tetrahedral shape with bond angle $109.5^\circ$.

$$\text{NH}_4^+ : \text{4 bond pairs, tetrahedral, } 109.5^\circ$$

**See what happens to form ammonia**

When $\text{NH}_4^+$ loses $\text{H}^+$, it becomes $\text{NH}_3$ with 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair. The lone pair repels more strongly and squeezes the angle down.

$$\text{NH}_3 : \text{3 bond pairs + 1 lone pair, pyramidal, } 107^\circ$$

**Find the shapes in the second conversion**

In $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$ each carbon is trigonal planar with 3 electron domains, so angles are about $120^\circ$. In $\text{C}_2\text{H}_6$ each carbon is tetrahedral with 4 single bonds, so angles are about $109.5^\circ$.

$$\text{C}_2\text{H}_4 (120^\circ) \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_6 (109.5^\circ)$$

**Spot the common feature**

Both conversions go from a larger bond angle to a smaller bond angle. That is a decrease in bond angle in both cases, so this is the shared feature.

options.A: Not shared. In $\text{NH}_4^+ \rightarrow \text{NH}_3$, nitrogen stays at oxidation state -3 in both. In $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4 \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_6$, carbon changes from -2 to -3. Only the second shows a change.
options.B: Correct. $\text{NH}_4^+$ ($109.5^\circ$) to $\text{NH}_3$ ($107^\circ$) is a decrease due to lone pair repulsion. $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$ ($\approx 120^\circ$) to $\text{C}_2\text{H}_6$ ($\approx 109.5^\circ$) is a decrease due to change from trigonal planar to tetrahedral. Both show a decrease.
options.C: Not shared. $\text{NH}_4^+ \rightarrow \text{NH}_3$ does create a lone pair on nitrogen. But $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4 \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_6$ forms only new C-H sigma bonds, no lone pair is formed on carbon.
options.D: Not shared. $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4 \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_6$ does lose the C=C pi bond to give a C-C single bond. But $\text{NH}_4^+ \rightarrow \text{NH}_3$ involves only sigma N-H bonds, there is no pi bond to lose.
